blocks.p: In the bottom drawer there were two bundles of washi, and between them lay a third sheet. It was the colour of rust.

Rei lifted it out by the edges. He knew what it was before he had it in the light. He had read about it in the glyph chapter the morning before, and he had hoped he would never see one, the way a person hopes about a lump. A self, closed and struck through. A mouth sealed, and the thing inside it burned. A door drawn shut over the body, ringed with locks. It was the most complex figure in Gin's book. It was drawn here in a brown that had once been red, by a hand that had not started to lean.

This was the Final Refusal. Gin's book explained it in a few hard lines. It is drawn in the maker's own blood and pressed over his own heart. When he finishes the last stroke, it ends him at once. A demon is refused the body, and whatever an enemy wanted from him burns with him. It can only ever be used on oneself.
It was finished except for one stroke. The last one. The one a person makes himself, over his own heart.

I have drawn it correctly twice, both times for others who asked, both times burned unused. There was no name on this one. There did not need to be. Gin had drawn it for himself, sometime in the last good weeks. Something had started thinning the wall toward him then. He had felt watched, and he had blamed the wrong thing. He had drawn the Refusal the way he drew everything, early and carefully, so it would be there if he needed it. Then he had put it in the drawer beside the circle that could save him. He had gone to work, and come home one Wednesday too tired to know he was tired.
Let it be me, he had said at the rail. I am already most of the way gone.

Rei stood at the kitchen sink with the sheet in one hand and the lighter in the other for a long time. The lighter was the cheap one he had carried for years. He turned it over in his fingers whenever he was waiting for something, and he only noticed now that he had been turning it all afternoon. Then he burned the Final Refusal over the drain and watched the brown figure curl up and go. Gin had drawn it twice for others, and both times it had burned unused. Rei made it three.

He packed Gin's field kit on the kitchen table, the way Gin had packed it in front of him a hundred times while Rei pretended to watch television. It looked like the kit of a man going camping. That was the point.

Threshold wards, folded into strips, went into the left front pocket, where Gin had kept them in every bag he owned. Three sealed vials of sulphur, small glass, unbroken, went on the left side. Then six prepared configurations from the desk, each in its own sleeve, each labelled in Gin's small print. He counted them twice and stopped at nine prepared glyphs in total. Gin had written that more than ten could be felt by anyone who was reading for them. Into the inside pocket of his jacket went the two washi bundles with the compass roses on them. They held the exorcism circle in five parts, each part sealed separately, two complete sets. In six years Gin had used one set once, after three months of preparation. Rei had had an afternoon.

He could not draw a single one of them. He had understood that while reading the chapter. Gin's post-it said it plainly. Studying this gives understanding. It does not give the hand. But the hand had already been given. Gin had given it, on a Monday morning with forty sheets of Kanda washi on the desk. I prepared more than I will use. I do not know why I did that today specifically. Rei thought he knew now. Part of Gin had been packing for this night before either of them knew it would come.
Last, because his hands would not do it any sooner, he took the folded Stability Mark out of his shirt pocket. He looked at the R. in the corner. Then he put it back over his heart.

He was sitting in the genkan with his shoes on when he remembered the page he had always skipped. It was near the end of the book, with a heading in Gin's tidy print. He had skipped it the first time because it looked like a list of types, the kind of thing a recruitment office would print.

doc.title: Gin's book. The Eight Patterns. How people come to this work
lines: A Saturday. Rei is playing video games. I am writing about the eight ways a person can begin to understand what they are, because no two practitioners find the veil through the same door.
Entry point is not class. It is starting position.
One. The Registered Practitioner. Official, inside the system. Access and surveillance in equal measure. Kato is Entry One. Adachi is Entry One.
Two. The Grid Operative. Unregistered. Network trust. Tanizaki is Entry Two. He has been Grid since before I was born.
Three. The Civilian Medium. Sensitive, unframed. The world just became very large.
Four. The Suppressed. Hiding what they are. Real rank at least two levels above what they show. The performance is the protection. This is the one I know best. I am aware that I am describing myself.
Five. The Institutional Enforcer. The system's instrument. Interesting when the system asks for the wrong thing.
Six. The Possessed. A good spirit sharing your body with your full awareness and consent.
Seven. The Witness. Zero rank or near it. Survives by being the person no one sees coming.
Eight. The Demon. A demon in a Vessel Program body, under formal contract with the CVD. You remember being human.
Rei is Entry Four. He does not know this yet. He will. Documentation is not exposure. It is care. G.U. A Sunday. Rei is in the next room.

blocks.p: Rei read the last line and laughed once, out loud, in the empty entrance, because it was so exactly like Gin to write a thing like that and then go and make dinner. Rei had been in the next room. He could almost remember the Sunday. He had been annoyed about something. He had had no idea, then, that he was being written down with love.

Entry Four. Hiding what they are. The performance is the protection. For six years Rei had performed being nothing much. A crime-scene temp with bad sleep and a headache habit. His brother had taught him to do it, at a kitchen table, as a trick for sleeping. Tonight, at the river, the performance would end. Whatever he was, he would be it in front of everything.
He thought about what the Healer had shown him all month without ever saying it. There were two ways to grow into a seat.

The first way was hunger. The grain the far shore had left in his palms was hungry. He could feel it. It wanted other people's registers the way a mouth wants bread. If he fed it, if he took in other people's feelings to grow fast, he would become strong very quickly. That was what a Qliphoth did. It ate a holder out from under a seat and wore the register like an empty shell.
The second way was the way the twelve did it. Hold one register open and steady with one's own self, sane and willing, every morning, for as long as it took. It was slower. It was the only clean way.
He closed his fists over the grain and did not feed it.
In the genkan, with his shoes on and three folded pages over his heart, the whole night stopped being an idea. It became a fact in his body, which is the only place ideas ever really land.

He could not be at the seam and at the chair and at his brother's side all at the same hour. By the cruelty of how this had been built, they were the same hour. And a body is one body in one place, even a body that can feel both sides of a wall. To put his hand on the wall was to take it off the chair. To reach for his brother was to leave the wall unread at the moment it could be written on. There was no way to arrange the night so that all his hands were where he wanted them. That was all the month-long dread had ever been. A simple animal fact, dressed up as something complicated, because complicated is bearable and a single forced step is not.

He thought about the twelve. Each of them must have stood once in a doorway like this, with their own pages folded over their own hearts, and gone out, and become what going out made them. Watanabe weakening. Mori Takao at his boiler for twenty years. Park Junho on his knees. None of them had got to hold every clock. That was what a seat cost, and what a wall cost, and, Rei understood now, what a brother cost. Not the price paid at the river, which would be loud and quick. This. The doors that close softly behind a person as he walks out of a flat, the ones he never gets to find out were the right ones.

The drums were louder now. The grey outside had turned to the deep blue that meant the festival's last night had begun. Up and down the ward people were carrying the small fires out to their doorsteps to send their dead home. Somewhere along the embankment his brother was already standing at the rail in his grey cardigan, looking at a doubled river, glad in two ways at once that Rei was coming.

Rei put his hand on the door. He did not feel ready. He had stopped believing that being ready had ever been possible. Instead he felt the thing Higuchi's smallest letters had really been about. It was not fear of the wall. It was the terrible privilege of being the one person who can feel both sides of a closing door, and who has to decide anyway which side to be on when it shuts.

He heard his own door click shut behind him. The sound was smaller than the thing it was, the way important sounds always are. That was the real foreclosure. Not the river. This small click. The flat with its three pages, and the version of the night where he stayed inside in the grey hour reading and never had to go. All of it sealed away behind the sound a key makes in a lock.
He went down through the streets toward the water, and the ward came out to meet him.

It was the night of okuribi, and the whole of Kita was outside. On every second doorstep a little fire of hemp stalks burned in a clay dish or a tin tray. Old men crouched over them in their undershirts, feeding the flames one stalk at a time. Families stood around in summer yukata and talked quietly to the smoke as if someone were standing in it. A girl of about six held her grandmother's hand and asked where the smoke was going. "Home," the grandmother said. Rei walked between the little fires. The heat of the day had not broken. Sweat ran down his back under the kit bag. Overhead a Keihin-Tōhoku train went by on its embankment, lit and full, its sky-blue stripe flashing between the roofs, carrying people home from work to their own small fires.

blocks.cap: The dead market arcade, shutters down

blocks.p: He passed the dead market arcade, two streets north of the market. Its shutters were down. Its storm drains breathed cold air into the August night. Gin's book called it a crossing point and said never stand over one you have not warded. Rei walked in the middle of the road.

Above the arcade, in a cheap flat, one window was lit. A man in a vest sat at it with his head in his hands. He had the look of someone who has been tired for a year and thinks it is only age. On the windowsill beside him stood a row of potted plants. All of them had died, but only on the side of the room nearest the arcade. The nameplate by the street door said Tachibana. Rei stopped dead on the tarmac. Then he made himself breathe. It was a common name. It was not the same man. It was only a tired stranger being slowly drained by the arcade beneath him, and Rei had no hour to give him tonight. He put the window away in his memory with all the others he meant to come back for.

He passed under the railway arches. Inside the third arch was Kemuri, a tiny bar with six stools and one red bulb, behind a door with no handle set into the brick. Its bartender, Goro, leaned beside the door with a cigarette, watching the festival go by. Goro looked at Rei's face, and then at the kit bag. He lifted two fingers from his cigarette in a kind of salute. He did not say anything. At Kemuri, nobody ever did.

blocks.cap: Nagai Haruto at the north bridge

blocks.p: At the north bridge a group of kids sat on the concrete steps above the water with cans and phones. They were loud and sitting too close to the edge. A boy of seventeen stood a little apart from them with his hands in his pockets. His black hair had a faded brown inch at the ends, and he was turning something over in one pocket. A river stone. This was Nagai Haruto. Rei knew the name from the ward's talk about the riverside kids. He was the one the others listened to.

As Rei watched, the boy glanced at a patch of water just downstream, as if someone there had spoken. Then he stepped between two of the others, a second before one of them would have shoved the other in. The water was quieter where he stood. Rei, with his registers half up, saw who stood in it with him. A small boy, wet to the shoulders, keeping watch on the same stretch of river, so that no other child would drown there and join him.

blocks.cap: The drowned boy who keeps watch beside him

blocks.p: Rei kept walking. Silently, he promised the two of them that he would come back.

Below the embankment, at the riverside memorial, the old woman in the flowered apron was setting out her lanterns. Her name was Okuma Sumi. Rei had heard it from Choi Hana, who read grief for a living and said she worried about the memorial keeper and did not know what to do. Mrs. Okuma looked frailer than she had the night before. She was setting out an extra lantern, the one she kept for the bad anniversaries. The memorial felt warmer with her there. Rei could feel the grief of the March ground leaning toward her the way the lanterns leaned toward the far bank. It was drinking from her, gently.

"You'll want to hurry," she said, without looking up. "The river's going a long way tonight. I've a mind to go with it one of these years. I gave my good umbrella to the girl next door this afternoon. She'll get more use of it."
Rei stopped. He did not have time. He stopped anyway.
"Will you be here tomorrow night?" he asked. "And the night after? My brother's going to need someone to light one for him. I don't know how. I've never done it right."
She looked up at him then, properly, with wet, kind eyes. For a moment the warmth around her seemed to hesitate.
"Somebody has to show you, then," she said slowly. "Don't they."
"Somebody has to," Rei said.

Ahead of him the river was doing what Higuchi's most frightened letters had promised. There were two banks where there should be one. Two cities a degree out of line. The seam between them was bright and soft, and it was thinning toward the hour all three of his clocks had been falling toward since the year the lights went grey.
He stopped once, at the turn of the path where he could see his brother. The grey cardigan. The rail. The two kinds of gladness already turning toward the sound of his shoes on the gravel.

And across the river, on the far embankment, it was not Kaito this time. It was a woman in her late thirties in a pale cardigan, with a few grey hairs left in on purpose. She stood very straight with her hands folded. Behind her, coming up the far steps in a slow, silent line, were thirty or more people in mourning clothes. Kanna-sensei had come herself.
Rei let his two suppressed registers come all the way up for the first time in a month. Both sides at once. No half measure. Half measures are for reading, and he was done reading.

The city went double and bright and unbearable and beautiful around him. The lanterns, and their held-breath shadows. The wall, and its soft thin wound. The brother and the Healer in one body. The thing in Fukai Rinka's body, smiling across the water with a dead woman's gentle face. And at the centre of it all, very far down, a tired man in an old coat with his back to the world, holding a door.
The three clocks touched the same hour. Rei stepped onto the embankment.
